items.title: Bartlett made the first noble gas compound in 1962
items.claim: Until 1962 every chemistry textbook said noble gases were entirely unreactive. Neil Bartlett at UBC noticed that O2's ionisation energy (1175 kJ/mol) almost matches xenon's (1170). PtF6 had stripped an electron from O2. So PtF6 should be able to oxidise xenon. He tried it. XePtF6 formed instantly.
items.prompt: Why did this single result change inorganic chemistry?

options.text: It broke the assumed inviolability of the noble-gas 'rule of full octets' and opened the chemistry of an entire group of elements that had been written off as inert

items.reveal:
Bartlett's noticed PtF6 (a deep red solid) turned air red on contact: PtF6 had oxidised O2 to O2+ PtF6-. He looked up xenon's ionisation energy, saw the near-equality with O2, and reasoned that PtF6 should also oxidise xenon.

The synthesis (Vancouver, March 1962) used a gas-handling apparatus he had built himself. Within months, Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produced XeF4 by simply heating xenon with fluorine at 400°C.

Today: XeF2, XeF4, XeF6, XeO3, XeO4, KrF2, ArF (the last only at cryogenic temperatures). Bartlett died in 2008. His insight made the chemistry of noble gases a real subject overnight.
items.why: Chemistry has 'laws' that turn out to be untested generalisations. A single decisive experiment can break a 70-year consensus.

items.title: Lithium has a stronger 'urge' to react than sodium — and reacts more gently
items.claim: Drop sodium into water: it fizzes violently, often igniting with a yellow flame. Drop lithium into water: it floats and fizzes calmly. Yet lithium's standard electrode potential (-3.04 V) is MORE negative than sodium's (-2.71 V).
items.prompt: Why doesn't lithium react more vigorously?

options.text: Lithium's high melting point (181°C) means it stays solid during reaction; the LiOH product is less soluble than NaOH and forms a coating that slows further reaction. Sodium melts in the reaction heat and exposes fresh surface
Standard electrode potentials are wrong for lithium
Lithium does not actually react with water

items.reveal:
Lithium's small ion has a very large hydration enthalpy (-519 kJ/mol vs sodium's -406), which more than compensates for its higher ionisation energy. So thermodynamically it has the highest tendency in Group 1 to lose an electron in aqueous solution.

But reactivity at the bench is rate-controlled by surface kinetics. Sodium melts at 98°C, well below the temperature reached during reaction with water — molten sodium spreads and exposes fresh metal. Lithium melts at 181°C and stays solid.

LiOH solubility is about 12 g per 100 g water; NaOH is 109 g. The lithium product crusts on the surface and slows further attack.
items.why: The reactivity series is taught as a single ladder. Real reactivity needs both thermodynamic driving force and a kinetic pathway.

items.title: Chromatography separates by retention, not by size
items.claim: Drop coloured ink on filter paper and dip the edge in water. The colours separate into bands. The colours that travel furthest aren't the smallest — they spend more time in the moving solvent and less time stuck to the paper.

options.text: Each component has its own equilibrium between the mobile phase (solvent) and the stationary phase (paper or silica); components that prefer the solvent travel fast, those that prefer the stationary phase travel slowly

items.reveal:
Rf = distance travelled by component / distance travelled by solvent front. Always between 0 and 1, characteristic of a molecule for a given solvent and stationary phase.

A polar molecule with many H-bond donors sticks to polar silica or paper and has Rf close to 0. A non-polar molecule prefers a non-polar solvent and has Rf close to 1.

This principle scales up to billion-dollar industrial chromatography for drug purification — same physics, bigger columns and more elaborate detectors. HPLC, GC, ion exchange and size exclusion all derive from the same competitive-equilibrium concept.
items.why: Chromatography is taught as 'big vs small'. The mechanism is competitive equilibrium between two phases — and that's what makes it so versatile.
